back: The straight-line distance from the start point to the current position, **with a direction**. A vector, in metres.
Velocity is the rate of change of **displacement** and has a direction (vector). Speed is the rate of change of distance — its magnitude only (scalar).
The rate of change of velocity: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$, in m s⁻². A vector.

front: On a velocity–time graph, what do the **gradient** and the **area** give you?
back: Gradient = acceleration. Area under the line = displacement.

Which suvat equation has **no time** in it?
Which suvat equation has **no final velocity** in it?
When are the suvat equations valid?
back: Only when the acceleration is **constant** (uniform) in size and direction.

front: What is the acceleration of free fall near the Earth’s surface?
back: $g \approx 9.8$ m s⁻², directed downwards — the same for all masses when air resistance is negligible.

front: At the top of a vertical throw, what is the acceleration?
back: Still $g$ downwards. Only the velocity is momentarily zero.

front: Launch speed $u$ at angle $\theta$ above horizontal: what are the components?
What links the horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile?
back: **Time.** The two motions are otherwise independent.

front: Why does a falling object reach terminal speed?
back: Drag increases with speed until it equals the weight. The resultant force is then zero, so the acceleration is zero and the speed stays constant.
